When we moved to the farm in the spring of 1962, the house had no electricity and the well water tasted of iron. My father spent the first summer rebuilding the barn, while my mother planted a vegetable garden that fed us through the winter. Every evening, we sat on the porch and listened to the radio, which ran on a large battery that my brother carried into town each Saturday to be recharged. Those years were hard, but I remember them as some of the happiest of my life.

Every morning, before the rest of the house was awake, my grandfather walked down to the harbour. He said the sea was easiest to understand when nobody else was talking. He would stand by the railing with a mug of tea, watching the fishing boats come in, and he could tell you which family each one belonged to just by the way it turned toward the dock. When I was nine, he started taking me with him. At first I was bored. I wanted to know why we were standing in the cold, doing nothing. He didn't answer. He just pointed at the water, at the gulls following the boats, at the old man mending nets on the far pier, and waited. It took me most of that summer to understand what he was showing me. Nothing in the harbour happened by accident. The tide decided when the boats could leave. The weather decided how far they could go. The gulls knew which boats had a good catch long before anyone on shore did. Everything was paying attention to everything else. Years later, after he had passed away, I went back to that railing on a grey October morning. The boats were different now, bigger and louder, and most of the families I remembered had sold up and moved inland. But the gulls still followed the boats in, and the tide still came and went, and for a few minutes, standing there with my own mug of tea, I could almost hear him not saying anything at all.
